as_told.title: Bob Jacobs recalls filming the Big Sur missile launch

plain: In September 1964, a test rocket called an Atlas was launched from Vandenberg Air Force Base in California carrying a dummy nuclear warhead, and on film a saucer-shaped object is said to have flown up to the warhead, circled it and fired beams of light at it until it tumbled off course. Bob Jacobs, an Air Force photo specialist who filmed it, tells it first hand. He says the launch "popped up through the fog," and that when the film was reviewed, "suddenly into that frame an object flew in chasing the warhead." Jacobs credits his supervisor, Major Florenze Mansmann, who Michels says backs the story. Michels tells the case many times, drawing on Robert Hastings's book UFOs and Nukes, and he cites Jacobs's DD214, a US military discharge record, as proof of his service. His details shift: he places Jacobs 100 miles up the coast at Big Sur with a telescope, gives speeds from 8,000 to 12,000 miles an hour, says "four directed energy beams" were fired, and says the film was taken away. The journalist Ross Coulthart, citing an Omni magazine article, says the film showed a UFO "shooting at it with a laser beam," though he puts the launch near Edwards Air Force Base. The filmmaker James Fox also brings it up. If true, something was able to track and disable a nuclear warhead in flight.
